overview.text: Morocco is a kingdom in northwestern Africa, with coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Its capital is Rabat, and its 2011 constitution describes a monarchy with a parliament and a head of government. Earlier Moroccan rulers dealt with European powers as sovereigns; Morocco and the United States signed a peace and friendship treaty in 1786. France established a protectorate over much of Morocco in 1912, while Spain controlled some areas. Morocco regained independence in 1956. Its location between the Atlantic, Mediterranean, and inland North Africa has long shaped its political and commercial connections.

overview.text: Charles de Gaulle was a French soldier and statesman whose leadership spanned World War II and the creation of the Fifth Republic. After France sought an armistice with Germany in 1940, he broadcast an appeal from London on 18 June urging French forces to continue fighting. He led the Free French movement and later headed France’s provisional government. De Gaulle returned to power during the Algerian crisis in 1958 and backed a new constitution approved by referendum. As president from 1959 to 1969, he oversaw Algerian independence and pursued a foreign policy that emphasized French autonomy.

overview.text: Former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe was fatally shot on 8 July 2022 while speaking at an election campaign event in Nara. The speech was for a candidate in an upcoming election to Japan’s upper house of parliament. Security officers seized a suspect at the scene; reporting identified him as Tetsuya Yamagami and described the weapon as homemade. Abe was taken to Nara Medical University Hospital, where he was pronounced dead later that day. The reported use of a handmade weapon drew attention in a country where strict firearms laws make buying a gun difficult.

overview.text: The Bay of Pigs invasion was a failed attempt in April 1961 to overthrow Fidel Castro’s government in Cuba. The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency trained and funded Cuban exiles organized as Brigade 2506; President John F. Kennedy approved the operation after inheriting the plan. The brigade landed on Cuba’s southern coast on 17 April and was defeated within two days by Cuban forces commanded by Castro. The failure strengthened Castro’s government and forced U.S. officials to rethink their Cuba policy. It also sharpened Cold War tensions: Soviet and American leaders exchanged messages about the invasion while Washington considered further covert action.

overview.text: Operation Car Wash, or Lava Jato, was a Brazilian investigation into corruption and money laundering that began in March 2014. Federal prosecutors first investigated networks involving public officials, businesspeople, and money dealers in Curitiba; related inquiries later spread to other states. Evidence and later corporate admissions exposed bribery connected to Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, as well as contractors and political figures. In one U.S. resolution, Petrobras acknowledged corrupt payments and false accounting. The case also reached construction firm Odebrecht and petrochemical company Braskem. Its wide reach made it a major episode in Brazil’s modern political and legal history.

overview.text: Thomas More was an English lawyer, humanist writer, and royal official under Henry VIII. His book Utopia, published in 1516, became an influential work of early modern writing. More served as Speaker of the House of Commons in 1523 and became lord chancellor in 1529. He resigned in 1532 as Henry’s break with papal authority advanced. More later refused an oath that affirmed the king’s supremacy over the English church, even though he accepted the new succession. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London, tried for treason, and executed in 1535.

overview.text: Inuit are Indigenous peoples whose Arctic homelands stretch across Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, and Chukotka in Russia. Their communities have distinct local languages and histories while sharing important ties across the circumpolar region. In Canada, the term Inuit Nunangat refers to four Inuit regions and includes land, water, and ice. Hunting and sharing country foods remain important to many families, alongside contemporary work in government, art, and other professions. The Inuit Circumpolar Council, founded in 1977, brings Inuit from the four regions together to advocate for rights, cultural continuity, and protection of the Arctic environment.

overview.text: New Zealand held two postal referendums in 2015 and 2016 to decide whether to replace its national flag. In the first vote, people ranked alternative designs; the leading choice was a black, white, and blue Silver Fern flag. The second vote, held in March 2016, put that design against the existing flag in a binding choice. The existing flag won with 56.6 percent of valid votes, so no change followed. The process illustrates a two-stage referendum: voters first selected a possible replacement and then decided whether to adopt it. The Electoral Commission recorded both the voting method and official results.

overview.text: Cleisthenes was an Athenian statesman whose reforms around 508 BCE helped lay the foundations of Athenian democracy. After the fall of the tyrant Hippias, he competed with Isagoras for influence and sought support from Athenian citizens. His reforms reduced the political importance of old family groupings by organizing citizens into local demes and ten new tribes. A council of 500 became a central institution in this system. These changes broadened participation among citizens, but citizenship itself remained limited, especially excluding women. The democracy associated with Cleisthenes developed further under later Athenian leaders, so he is best understood as a founder of its institutions rather than its final form.

overview.text: The Tet Offensive was a coordinated series of attacks by North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces in South Vietnam beginning during the lunar New Year holiday in late January 1968. Major fighting reached cities including Saigon and Huế, and attackers breached the outer walls of the U.S. Embassy compound in Saigon. U.S. and South Vietnamese forces eventually retook lost ground, inflicting severe losses on the attackers. Yet the scale and surprise of the offensive undermined claims that victory was near and weakened public support for the war in the United States. Its military and political effects therefore pointed in different directions.
